I think things make a lot more sense once you understand how money is created. Sure the Fed can lend the government money through bond purchases, but where did that money come from? Fractional reserve banking is the answer. You can find a million hits on YouTube or whatever for 'how is money created' but I can give you a really succinct synopsis:

  • Let's pretend the only person with any money in the world is Joe, who has $100.
  • Joe deposits his $100 at the bank.
  • In fractional reserve banking, banks need only keep 10% of deposits on hand. So the bank is free to lend out $90.
  • Sue borrows $90 and eventually spends it, transferring it to James.
  • James deposits $90 in the bank. The bank now keeps 10% of that deposit and lends out the rest, or $81.
  • Robert borrows $81 from the bank and eventually spends it, transferring it to Kim.
  • So forth and so on.

Think about what just happened above. The only "real" money in the world is Joe's $100. Yet somehow now there are deposits in the bank for $100, $90, and $81 or $271. And that's just getting started. In total $100 of real money will create $1000 of new money that's created through the issuance of debt. And since banks charge interest on their loans, it'll actually create far more than $1000 of new money and debt. Interestingly, there is literally not enough money in the world to pay off all debt in this system - not even remotely close. Keep in mind there is still only $100 of "real money" in this world. If even a small fraction of depositors at this bank tried to cash out the money wouldn't exist and the bank would need to get a loan from the central bank aka "The Federal Reserve" or Fed in the USA.

And that role is one of many that brings them into the picture. Keeping this whole charade acting like a currency is the purpose of the Fed and based on the evidence they seem to do a fine job. Our economy today is a vastly more connected, complex, interdependent, and consequently vulnerable than it was in the 19th century and prior. Yet it's at least as stable and arguably substantially more so. This all deserves a lot more discussion (especially on inflation vs deflation), but this is already getting a bit lengthy. I think once you understand how money is made, and once you get a good grasp on the effect of inflation vs deflation, the purpose of the Fed becomes much more clear.
